title: Why a peak is broad or shifted
key_message: Hydrogen bonding broadens O–H and N–H; salts give broad bands between 3200 and 2300; the solid and the crystal shift peaks.
body: When an O–H or N–H forms [[hydrogen-bond|hydrogen bonds]] with neighbouring molecules, each molecule vibrates a little differently and the peak broadens. [[amine-salt|Salts]] (for example hydrochlorides) have an N–H with a positive charge that gives a very broad band between 3200 and 2300. The crystal form and the water in the crystal also shift peaks: the same substance as a salt or as a [[free-base|base]] has two different spectra.
The figure shows two demonstration spectra of the same molecule: the salt form and the free base.
for_chemists: Hydrogen bonding: free alcoholic O–H 3620–3670 (narrow), associated 3200–3500 (broad); carboxylic acid dimer 2500–3300, very broad. [[conjugation|Conjugation]] lowers the C=O by about 30–40 cm⁻¹ (saturated ketone 1715, α,β-unsaturated 1685, aromatic 1690); [[ring-strain|ring strain]] raises it (cyclohexanone 1715, cyclopentanone 1750, cyclobutanone 1785).

[[fermi-resonance|Fermi resonance]]: an overtone or combination close in energy to a fundamental splits it in two (aldehydes: C–H doublet at ~2820 and ~2720). Amine salts: primary ~3200–2800, secondary ~3000–2700, tertiary ~2700–2300, with combination bands between 2800 and 2000; NH₃⁺ bend 1625–1560 and 1550–1500, NH₂⁺ 1620–1560, none for NH⁺.

In the gas phase bands show rotational structure; in liquids and solids they do not. In crystals, packing and [[polymorphism|polymorphism]] matter. The pair in the figure is a proposal of the service made with FTIR (cocaine hydrochloride and cocaine base), not confirmed with other techniques.

figure.alt: Two demonstration absorbance spectra, from 4000 to 500 cm⁻¹: the salt form (solid line) has a broad envelope between 3200 and 2300 cm⁻¹ that the free base (dashed line) lacks. The interval is highlighted.
figure.caption: Salt and free base of the same molecule: the broad N–H⁺ band is the most visible difference.
